questions.q: What are the four criteria explicitly referenced in UN General Assembly Resolution 60/1 (2005 World Summit Outcome) for new permanent members of the Security Council?
questions.a: The four criteria are: (1) contribution to the maintenance of international peace and security, (2) contribution to the UN budget, (3) population size, and (4) level of democracy and respect for human rights. A wrong answer listing "nuclear capability" or "GDP ranking" reveals the student is conflating India's self-justification with the formally agreed UN criteria — a common error where students memorise India's talking points instead of the actual UN benchmark.

questions.q: Why does the "Uniting for Consensus" (UfC) group oppose new permanent seats but support longer-term non-permanent seats?
questions.a: UfC (led by Italy, Pakistan, South Korea, Canada, etc.) argues that adding permanent members entrenches privilege and undermines sovereign equality; they prefer a reformed category of longer-term (e.g., 4-5 year), immediately re-eligible non-permanent seats to ensure rotation and accountability. A wrong answer claiming "UfC opposes all reform" shows the student misses the nuance: UfC supports expansion but rejects the *permanent* tier — a distinction critical for board questions on "nature of opposition."

questions.q: Apply the Charter amendment procedure (Articles 108 and 109) to explain why Security Council reform requires a two-thirds UNGA majority *plus* ratification by all P5 members.
questions.a: Article 108 requires amendments to be adopted by two-thirds of UNGA members and ratified by two-thirds of member states *including all permanent members of the Security Council*. Since reform alters Chapter V (Composition), it triggers Article 108. Article 109 allows a General Conference but still requires P5 ratification. A wrong answer citing only "two-thirds UNGA vote" ignores the P5 ratification veto — the single biggest procedural hurdle, making China's consent indispensable for India.

questions.q: Compare the African Group's "Ezulwini Consensus" position with the G4 position on veto power for new permanent members.
questions.a: The Ezulwini Consensus (African Union) demands *full veto power* for new permanent members from day one, arguing anything less creates second-class permanence. G4 (India, Brazil, Germany, Japan) has signaled willingness to *forgo veto for 15-20 years* as a confidence-building measure. A wrong answer stating "both want veto immediately" misses the strategic divergence: Africa sees veto as non-negotiable equity; G4 sees veto-delay as political pragmatism to break P5 deadlock.

questions.q: Evaluate the argument: "India's peacekeeping contribution alone justifies its permanent seat." Use at least two other criteria to support or refute.
questions.a: The argument is *necessary but insufficient*. Peacekeeping (criterion 1) is India's strongest claim — 2,75,000+ troops since 1948, highest cumulative. But the 2005 criteria require *all four* dimensions. India's per capita GDP ($2,400) and HDI rank (134th) weaken the "economic strength" and "development" dimensions compared to P5. A strong answer acknowledges peacekeeping as *necessary condition* but notes India must also demonstrate *normative leadership* (democracy, human rights) and *financial capacity* (budget share ~0.83% vs P5's 3-22%). A wrong answer treating peacekeeping as *sufficient* shows inability to apply multi-criteria evaluation.

questions.q: Draft a 150-word position paper for India's UN Mission proposing a "phased veto" model: new permanent members exercise veto only on Chapter VII enforcement actions after a 15-year review, subject to P5+new members consensus. Justify each element.
questions.a: A strong answer will: (1) cite Article 27(3) veto scope, (2) reference G4's 2005 "veto restraint" pledge, (3) link 15-year review to UN75 declaration's call for "revitalised multilateralism," (4) propose consensus mechanism to prevent unilateral veto expansion, (5) frame as bridge between Ezulwini (immediate veto) and P5 (no new veto). Poor answers omit Charter basis, ignore P5 ratification reality, or fail to address China/Pakistan opposition — revealing inability to design politically feasible reform.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The reform of the UN Security Council refers to the ongoing diplomatic and ______ process to restructure the Council's membership, working methods, and veto provisions to reflect 21st-century geopolitical realities rather than the 1945 power configuration.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you are India's Permanent ______ at the UN General Assembly in 2024, drafting a speech for the Intergovernmental Negotiations on Security Council reform.

Fill in the blank: India's claim for a permanent seat rests on its status as the world's largest democracy, fifth-largest economy, largest contributor to UN peacekeeping, nuclear-weapon state, and representative of the Global South, seeking to correct the Council's lack of equitable geographical representation mandated by UN Charter Article ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can evaluate India's candidacy against the four established criteria (contribution to UN, population, democracy, economic strength) and explain how the veto reform debate intersects with Charter amendment procedures under Articles 108 and 109.
